#3509. iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2182 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me.
  • But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m right now using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….
  • The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m right now using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Sources indicate that yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

What I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

It has been revealed that the size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

Sources indicate that my preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m right now viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen.

In a recent development, while the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I noted when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

Sources indicate that it’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an glitch at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI ).

The newly introduced gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

Sources indicate that I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

Sources indicate that the aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Recent findings suggest that finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

In a recent development, I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the new Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

Industry observers note that the Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

In a recent development, perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The problem is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

The rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the problem, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

One of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite promptly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller issue than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

I remarked in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

Sources indicate that I’m where you are. I received mine on Tuesday. It’s too heavy. It’s too expensive, especially with a subpar. Touch ID is annoying. The larger screen is going to be rarely used in my day-to-day. Giving up the larger main screen for a screen I’ll rarely use for an extra $1000 seems kinda dumb.

But every so often I open an app or webpage on the larger screen and it’s pretty amazing.

I’ll probably return it. But my choice isn’t the duo or the 18 Pro. By doing away with the iPhone upgrade program and not releasing a pro phone with groundbreaking advancements Apple has removed my incentive to move to the 18. If I send the Duo back I’ll keep my 17 Pro, and see what the Air 2 offers. Much like I moved from the larger, heavier MBP to the smaller, lighter MBA when its power far surpassed what I need I may do the same with my phone if the next gen of the iPhone Air is compelling enough.

Recent findings suggest that my head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Industry observers note that even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

It has been revealed that in previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

Review: Aqara W200 supports Adaptive Temperature in HomeKit at a great price

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year, my wife and I bought our first house.
  • One of the most crucial and useful smart home accessories is a smart thermostat.
  • Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, my wife and I bought our first house. Along with all the other exciting things, it’s also let me spend a lot of time testing fresh smart home gear.

One of the most crucial and useful smart home accessories is a smart thermostat. Six months ago, I installed the Aqara Smart Thermostat W200, and it’s been a fantastic addition to our smart home setup … especially because it supports Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature. Here’s how it works.

Installing the Aqara W200 was relatively straightforward. I’d previously installed various Ecobee thermostats. The trickiest part this time was learning the intricacies of the new house itself, which the Aqara app did a good job of guiding me through.

Sources indicate that I used the Aqara app for the installation and setup, like choosing an interface design for the thermostat’s display itself. But after that, I closed the app and haven’t opened it since. Everything now is managed through the Apple Home app, and I appreciate that the Aqara app lets me do this without any pushback. It doesn’t try to pull me back into it to sell me a subscription or show me ads.

Industry observers note that this matters because the Aqara app is nothing to write home about. It has a lot of settings, but I don’t think it’s particularly elegant or user-friendly. You can choose from a small collection of different screensavers. The thermostat’s interface is similar to the app in that it’s very utilitarian, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing for quick manual temperature adjustments.

The Aqara W200 also has a mmWave radar sensor that detects your presence. When you walk up to it, that sensor detects your approach and the screensaver automatically goes away to reveal the controls. It’s also exposed to HomeKit and can trigger automations. Unfortunately, this isn’t particularly useful for me because of the thermostat’s awkward location.

Sources indicate that the Aqara W200’s build quality is good enough. It’s primarily made of plastic, unlike higher-end smart thermostats that feature metal housing, so it doesn’t look super premium on your wall. It has a responsive 4-inch touchscreen. It has a small footprint overall, so you’ll likely need the included back trim plate if your previous thermostat required a larger opening in the wall.

According to recent reports, the standout feature of the Aqara W200, though, is its support for Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature, which debuted as part of iOS 26. As of right now, the Aqara W200 is the only thermostat with Adaptive Temperature support available, though two more are coming next year as part of Apple’s newly introduced Home Collection suite.

Recent findings suggest that adaptive Temperature is Apple’s feature that will automatically adjust your thermostat’s temperature based on your preferences. It uses your location and the location of other home members to determine when to adjust the thermostat.

Once you enable Adaptive Temperature, you set your ideal temperature range for the following states:.

Sources indicate that my wife and I set our preferred temperature ranges for each scenario. I particularly appreciate the ability to set a different range for night, since we like it noticeably colder overnight than during the day.

After that setup process, Adaptive Temperature has worked in the background without any involvement from us. It passively uses all the information on our iPhones to make its decision.

“Your iPhone uses on-device intelligence to predict when you’re on your way home to bring it to the correct temperature by the time you get there, and adjusts the thermostat to save energy when you are far away from home,” Apple explains.

Adaptive Temperature uses your iPhone and other home members’ devices to determine when to adjust the temperature. “Home can learn daily routines to predict when you’re likely to arrive and adjust the temperature for you,” Apple says. This includes things like your calendar events.

I can count on one hand the number of times we’ve had to manually adjust the thermostat since installing the W200, and most of those times were because we had guests with different preferences than ours.

Recent findings suggest that honestly, I thought I wrote this post months ago, but I guess it slipped my mind. I actually think there’s a pretty simple explanation for that, though. I installed the W200, enabled Adaptive Temperature in the Apple Home app, and haven’t thought about it since.

Sources indicate that I think that’s a great endorsement of the Aqara W200 as a product.   • The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit in a California court on Friday, striking back after the iPhone maker accused the AI lab of stealing top-secret information this summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI has countersued Apple, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets and threatening suppliers working on its upcoming devices. The filing escalates a legal fight that began with Apple’s lawsuit against OpenAI in July.

OpenAI has launched a upcoming legal action against Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers, in an effort to “compete unfairly by any means available”.

The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit in a California court on Friday, striking back after the iPhone maker accused the AI lab of stealing top-secret information this summer.

According to recent reports, according to the report, OpenAI alleges Apple is “coercing and threatening” suppliers working with the ChatGPT maker. Its hardware ambitions include upcoming personal devices following last year’s acquisition of Jony Ive’s “io” firm.

The complaint also claims Apple encouraged employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud accounts. OpenAI has previously characterized Apple’s case as an attempt to stop it from hiring Apple employees.

In a recent development, apple’s original lawsuit names OpenAI, io Products, and former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan. Tan previously led iPhone and Apple Watch product design at Apple.

Industry observers note that apple alleges confidential engineering information and hardware development details were taken to benefit OpenAI’s consumer device efforts. OpenAI has disputed those allegations.

The fresh action also follows OpenAI’s October claim that an employee who returned to Apple sent more than 100 confidential files about unreleased OpenAI hardware to personal accounts. Those files allegedly included device images, engineering data, and supplier information.

Apple responded at the time that its investigation had not located OpenAI confidential information. The organization said it requested more specific information to continue searching and would work with OpenAI to investigate the allegations.

Meanwhile, Apple has sought a preliminary injunction to prevent further use of its alleged trade secrets and won expanded access to evidence during discovery.

Apple’s original case is scheduled to go to trial on July 19, 2027.

Following publication, Apple shared the following statement with 9to5Mac:.

“This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple’s secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.”.

Tech Report: HomeKit Weekly: Meross’s upcoming presence sensor splits a room into three zones for Apple Home

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • You’ll set the zones in the Meross iPhone app during setup, choosing a distance for each.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that presence sensors tell Apple Home when someone is in a particular room, which is awesome for running automations based on that. They don’t tell it where in the room you are, though. That’s why these types of automations end up being all-or-nothing type things: you walk into a room, and every light comes on at full brightness, whether you came in to read at your desk or to grab something off the counter. The Meross MS605 splits its detection range into three distance zones, and each of them shows up in Apple Home as its own presence sensor so you can build automations around them.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

You’ll set the zones in the Meross iPhone app during setup, choosing a distance for each. Once the Meross MS605 is in Apple Home (via Matter), all three appear as separate presence sensors, and you can build automations for each individually. If you only want two, disable the third in the Meross app, and it disappears from the Home app as well.

A bathroom is the obvious use case here for early mornings. Set the far zone to turn a lamp on at 5% and the near zone to bring up an overhead light, etc.

It has been revealed that the same idea works anywhere the room has more than one job. A hallway can light the path dim from the far zone, then go to 100% when you get close. An office can keep the overheads on while you’re anywhere in the room and turn on the desk lamp when you actually sit down as well. I find it incredibly useful for overall dimming, though.

The Meross MS605 uses mmWave radar and PIR together, which is the current best practice for presence detection. Meross says the radar picks up micro-movement, so it knows you’re there when you’re sitting still, and the PIR filters out things that move but aren’t warm, like curtains and a robot vacuum. There’s also a radar-only setting if you want it as well.

Range is up to about 20 feet for motion and 13 feet for presence, with each zone configurable within those limits. There’s a built-in light sensor, too, so you can gate your lighting automations based on actual room brightness instead of guessing when you’ll want it with a sunset/sunrise trigger.

The Meross MS605 is IP67-rated and operates from -4 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, so a covered porch, a garage, or a basement is all fair game for placing the sensor.

According to recent reports, the initial setup runs via the Meross app over Bluetooth, and the app is required afterward. Zones, sensitivity, presence-and-absence timing, recalibration, and firmware updates all live in it. Day-to-day control and automation happen in Apple Home, but anything you want to tune requires going back.

One minor thing to know before you mount somewhere hard to reach: changing settings over Bluetooth requires pressing a physical button on top of the sensor, so keep that in mind when configuring your settings and initially placing it.

According to recent reports, the Meross MS605 unlocks some unique use cases with its three zones. Three zones from one sensor is a latest automation tool, and the IP67 rating means you can put it in places other presence sensors can’t go. It’s powered by a CR123A battery, which is included in the box.

The Meross MS605 is available on Amazon.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1730 w)

Review: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is an iPad alternative I actually want to use

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I knew Amazon’s fresh flagship tablet was different when I found myself actually reaching for it.
  • Industry observers note that of course, you might be saying, that’s the job of a reviewer: to use the device throughout your daily life and let people know the good, the bad, and the ugly.
  • The original Kindle Fire rolled out back when I was in high school, and despite 15 years of product name changes, frequent model refreshes, and an attempt to slowly move up-market, even Amazon’s bottom-of-the-barrel pricing couldn’t make up for missing apps and terrible performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I knew Amazon’s fresh flagship tablet was different when I found myself actually reaching for it.

Industry observers note that of course, you might be saying, that’s the job of a reviewer: to use the device throughout your daily life and let people know the good, the bad, and the ugly. But with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I wasn’t just reaching for it when I thought a tablet might do the job. Over the past two weeks since receiving my review unit (the base nanomatte model), I’ve been pleasantly surprised by just how much I’ve preferred it over other devices. Hell, I’ve been reaching for Amazon’s slate over my Pixel 11 Pro XL, my MacBook Air, and even the pocket-friendly Lenovo Legion tablet I reviewed earlier this month, and considering this firm’s history with tablets, I’m as shocked as anyone.

The original Kindle Fire rolled out back when I was in high school, and despite 15 years of product name changes, frequent model refreshes, and an attempt to slowly move up-market, even Amazon’s bottom-of-the-barrel pricing couldn’t make up for missing apps and terrible performance. But the Fire lineup is dead, replaced by a newly introduced lineup of more expensive “Alexa Tablets” that, nevertheless, remain a relative bargain in our ever-worsening gadget economy. This model, though, is a true iPad competitor. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro attempts to correct every mistake Amazon has made with its tablet series over the past fifteen years, and somehow, for as low as $350 on sale, it basically pulls it all off.

Industry observers note that let’s get some of the most crucial changes out of the way immediately before we get to the real star of the show. Most of Amazon’s specs sheet here won’t impress you, but context really means everything. A Mediatek Dimensity 8400 chipset paired with (in my test model) 8GB of RAM and 128GB of UFS 3.1 storage sounds like any run-of-the-mill midrange Android tablet. That’s a massive leap ahead of anything powering previous Fire Tablet models, though, and the option to move to a 256GB model with UFS 4.0 and 16GB of RAM does exist if you really feel like you need some extra power. This is also a completely unsubsidized tablet; regardless of which model you pick, you won’t have to pay $20 to remove lockscreen ads, something that remains an issue on the cheaper Alexa Tablet 8 and 11 models.

Sources indicate that honestly, both the design and the overall feel of the hardware exceed my expectations; this is closer to Apple or Samsung’s premium tablet offerings than it is the Fire Tablets of yesteryear. It features an aluminum chassis with rounded edges and a thin, flat frame that — let’s be honest — looks right out of Apple’s typical iPad playbook. The power button doubles as a fingerprint sensor, while an indented groove below the volume buttons on the right side for its optional stylus. As someone who thinks this slate is better off for consumption than creation, it’s the one part of the design I question, though it also didn’t really bother me.

Without a doubt, the star of the show is this display. Amazon sent me the nanomatte version, available as a $50 upgrade over the $500 MSRP base model (the $650 256GB variant only comes in nanomatte). If you’re thinking of buying this tablet, the nanomatte model is without a doubt the one to spring for. It’s one of the nicer matte finishes I’ve seen on a device like this to date, and is absolutely the main reason I won’t stop reaching for this tablet. With a couple of tweaks — the saturation levels are a little too punchy out of the box for my liking, but Amazon’s “natural” color profile is a two-tap fix — this is as good as any non-OLED screen I can think of in recent memory. In fact, where Lenovo’s LCD panel had me wishing for next year’s rumored upgrade, I really never felt like OLED needed to be on Amazon’s flagship slate to make it worth my while.

No matter what I loaded up — The Odyssey, various episodes of TV or YouTube videos, the unofficial “Dusklight” port of Twilight Princess for Android — I just kept wanting to stare at this thing. I now totally understand why people spring for the nanomatte iPad Pro, and while I’m not trying to say this LCD holds a candle to one of the best OLED screens on the market right now, it’s nice to get this sort of finish on a tablet that doesn’t start at a whopping $1,800. (The iPad Pro itself starts at $1,200, but nanomatte is only available on 1TB or 2TB models, which I didn’t know until I sat down to write this review and is absolutely one of the dumbest things I’ve ever seen a manufacturer of Apple’s size do. I digress.).

Amazon’s quad-stereo speakers sound excellent for a device of this size. They get surprisingly loud without much distortion, perfect for YouTube videos or streaming random movies, or even casual music listening. I’d still opt for headphones or external speakers for something you really care about (once again, The Odyssey being the perfect example), but that’s not exactly rare for a tablet. The fingerprint sensor is fast and mostly accurate, and the flashless 13MP rear-facing camera is… here, should you desperately need one. A more useful 8MP front-facing camera runs along the right side of the device, and there’s a single USB-C port at the bottom of the slate. No expandable storage options, something I’m genuinely disappointed about considering this slate tops out at just 256GB.

In a recent development, of course, we have to address the Amazon-sized elephant in the room: the software. Unlike the “Fire OS” fork of Android that has resulted in years of Christmas morning Google searches to find out how to get YouTube on the tablet you just unwrapped, the Alexa Tablet is just… running Android. That includes some obvious quality-of-life improvements, like being able to transfer apps and other data directly from your phone or an older tablet, but yes, it also means the Play Store is here, along with practically every Android app you could hope for. Gmail, Chrome, Docs, Photos — everything’s here, and the ability to no longer have to hope that a good-enough replacement exists on the Amazon Appstore is such a relief. Hell, Amazon’s own app marketplace isn’t even pre-installed.

According to recent reports, now, with all of that mentioned, there are a couple of weird software quirks you should know going in. First, you’ll likely find a handful of applications unlisted from the Play Store as “unsupported” apps. This includes Amazon’s own software — the pre-loaded Amazon app is, bizarrely, just a web wrapper for the typical browser experience — and a smattering of random third-party applications, including the launcher Lawnchair, which I installed via the APK hosted on its website. That’s the second quirk: the default launcher is, as you might expect, themed around both Amazon and Alexa, complete with two unremovable widgets. It’s far from the worst home screen experience I’ve ever had, but a third-party launcher from the Play Store (or, again, from somewhere on the web) solves that problem. Save for the rare appearance of Amazon’s own dock and Alexa search bar when swiping back home, the third-party launcher experience here is great.

Industry observers note that one more quick software positive: Amazon says it’ll support this tablet, along with the cheaper Alexa Tablet 11, through seven years of OS upgrades and security updates. We’ll have to see how frequent those updates arrive, but still — this experience feels built to last in a way Fire Tablets explicitly were not.

Sources indicate that the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s specs might not sound particularly impressive on paper, but I’ve had absolutely no performance complaints. Granted, I haven’t exactly pushed the envelope here — that Zelda shout-out is the most I’ve demanded graphically — but web pages loaded fast without crashes or reloads, apps stayed alive in the background, and moving around the OS generally felt snappy. If this bar sounds low, you probably never used a legacy Fire Tablet. Battery life, meanwhile, has been excellent, with a single charge typically getting me through a few days of mixed use. Charging speeds could be better, though, with a full charge taking nearly two hours to power the slate back up. That’s not enough reason to skip out on Amazon’s tablet, obviously, but it is one of those advantages that Samsung’s (much) more expensive Galaxy Tab S-series holds over it.

It’s possible that my excitement over Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro comes from a place of lowered expectations. I’m sure that’s true to some extent; again, 15 years of mostly-miserable experiences, up to and including the last time the company swung for a more premium slate, will do that to you. But considering Google’s disinterest in developing its own tablets and Samsung’s increasingly-ludicrous pricing for its higher-end options, I think this Alexa Tablet delivers a great alternative. Its specs are more than enough for the average Android user, and the things that I think people really care about on tablets — its display and its speakers — are among the best you can buy right now. Unless you really want to move into a four-figure price range for an OLED-equipped iPad or Galaxy Tab, I don’t really see a reason to shop around. And believe me, I’m still shocked.

It has been revealed that that’s especially true during Black Friday, which — despite this tablet launching just weeks prior — is deeply discounted for the holiday season. You can grab the base model Alexa Tablet 12 Pro for just $350, but you should spring for the nanomatte model at $400. That’s $150 off a price I already think isn’t terrible for the money, and frankly, an even stronger recommend if and when you can score it on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a phone that heavily tested my patience in the first few weeks, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has become an all-time favorite.
  • The amount of hype this phone brought with it at launch was unreal.
  • Recent findings suggest that I still believe the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is an excellent device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a phone that heavily tested my patience in the first few weeks, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has become an all-time favorite.

The amount of hype this phone brought with it at launch was unreal. Even then, I ultimately wound up going with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra of the two models Samsung released earlier this year. It’s a form factor I was used to, but only looking back now do I realize just how much I was missing out on.

Recent findings suggest that I still believe the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is an excellent device. But the widely accepted blueprint for a consumer foldable might make a lateral move to what the Galaxy Z Fold 8 offers. That, I wouldn’t mind.

In a recent development, by comparison, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is tiny. Its front display is squared-up and offers less vertical real estate than any other mainstream device coming out of Samsung. But that’s even more true compared to the lengthy profile the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has. It’s called a “candy-bar foldable” for a reason.

In a recent development, the entire way I used my phone had to change, and the first few times I used the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I was left with a slightly bad taste in my mouth. I genuinely didn’t enjoy using it because of the amount of friction I was running into – not because the phone caused it, but because of my contradicting usage habits.

Sources indicate that I always felt like I was missing out on something with the smaller front display, and I stubbornly tried to use the inner display in its wide orientation for most applications. I considered switching back, but I’m glad I stuck with it.

On the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or other standard foldables, I find myself using the inner display as the “main” display more often than not. But the Z Fold 8 gave me enough screen space in its closed state to come away with a good experience.

Industry observers note that since release, the majority of apps I use have been optimized in Android 17, or One UI 9. Social apps work well because that little bit of extra width leaves breathing room for videos to expand and fill the screen. Shopping and productivity apps are similar, and everything seems to fall into place.

It has been revealed that I hit a wall with the inner display, too. It took some time for me to realize using the Fold 8 in landscape was genuinely the wrong choice 70% of the time. It sounds weird, but a phone that was designed to open up to a wider inner screen offers a better experience when you rotate it. At that point, you’re getting the best part of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, without the other cons.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, the wide inner display is great for videos and multitasking – not as good as the Ultra. But the inner display in its relative portrait orientation is excellent on hand for apps that need a little more room. It essentially boils down to whether you want a significant screen for what you’re using the outer display for – a crazy thought, but not always the user experience.

Now, the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display feels like the new normal to me, and using another phone feels foreign. The inner display has its place, and I automatically rotate it for nearly everything but media.

Even if this phone were just a proof of concept, it was successful. These smaller devices can work with some getting used to.

It has been revealed that if given the choice between the design of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra once again, I’d now choose the smaller, wider Fold 8. Sure, it has a less capable camera loadout. The user experience does more to outweigh my ability to snap telephoto pictures, though.

This is a phone that has performed phenomenally in every major area, including how well it runs apps on Android and in battery life. I’m still getting more than a day’s worth of charge several months into using it. The same can’t be noted for the Galaxy Z Fold 7.

Industry observers note that it’s possible Samsung is working on a next-gen Galaxy Z Fold 9 with the build of the Fold 8 and the camera power of an “Ultra” model, but there’s nothing concrete. Until then, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is riding the wave it created.

#3477. Apple faces potential $80 million fine and App Store overhaul in Chile

Apple faces potential $80 million fine and App Store overhaul in Chile

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chile’s national competition authority, Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the organization of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases.
  • As reported by Reuters, Chile’s competition watchdog is seeking an $80 million fine against Apple, along with a court order requiring a series of changes to the company’s App Store policies.
  • In its complaint, the FNE says (translation ours):.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chile’s national competition authority, Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the organization of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases. Here are the details.

As reported by Reuters, Chile’s competition watchdog is seeking an $80 million fine against Apple, along with a court order requiring a series of changes to the company’s App Store policies.

In its complaint, the FNE says (translation ours):.

The defendant has violated Article 3, paragraphs one and two, subsection (b), of Decree Law 211 by abusing its dominant position through practices that prevent, restrict, or hinder free competition, or have the potential to do so, in the markets for app distribution and the distribution of paid digital goods within apps, both on the iOS operating system nationwide, from at least 2019 to the present day.

The FNE goes on to say that Apple forbids both sideloading and alternative app marketplaces, requires app developers to exclusively use the company’s In-App Purchase system to sell digital goods and services within their apps, and restricts their ability to inform customers about or direct them to alternative payment methods.

It then goes on to claim that “these anticompetitive practices have allowed the defendant to ensure that the App Store is the only channel for downloading apps,” adding that this “has led to a degradation of the consumer experience and allowed Apple to secure profits that it would not obtain without such practices.”.

Throughout the 50-page filing, the FNE draws on regulatory and judicial precedents from other jurisdictions, some involving ongoing disputes, to support its arguments that Apple’s restrictions are anticompetitive and that its privacy and security objectives can be achieved through less restrictive means.

That includes Apple’s agreement with Brazil’s competition authority, the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, the Epic Games v. Apple ruling in Australia, regulatory and judicial developments in Japan, and the lifting of anti-steering restrictions in the US.

At one point, the FNE even suggests that Apple knowingly maintained anticompetitive practices in the country, despite regulatory and judicial developments elsewhere:.

Furthermore, there is evidence suggesting that the defendant was aware of the unlawfulness of its conduct, given the existence of precedents in other jurisdictions involving facts similar to those alleged in this complaint, which demonstrate the anticompetitive nature of the alleged practices. Nevertheless, Apple decided to maintain its restrictions in Chile, as well as in other jurisdictions where it has not been compelled to remove them or has not agreed with the relevant authority to eliminate or modify them.

After presenting its case, the FNE asks Chile’s antitrust court to:.

Additionally, the FNE asks the court to require Apple to implement these measures “in good faith, such that it may not impose any other technical or contractual restrictions, or commercial conditions, that undermine their purpose,” to cease the alleged anticompetitive practices, and to cover the legal costs of the proceedings.

It also leaves room for the court to impose any additional measures it deems appropriate, particularly those aimed at facilitating access to alternative channels for app distribution and the sale of digital goods.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and will upgrade this post if the company responds.

You can read the FNE’s full complaint here (in Spanish).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dutch developer Jordi Bruin rolled out an patch to his excellent transcription app MacWhisper this week with a much-requested feature: the ability to automatically identify previously named speakers in latest recordings. Here are the details.

I’ve written multiple times in the past couple of years about how MacWhisper has become an integral part of my podcast post-production workflow for show notes, episode descriptions, and more.

Which is why I’ve followed the app’s development very closely, and Jordi’s efforts to make it an increasingly powerful tool for casual and power users alike.

In the last few months alone, MacWhisper got a completely redesigned transcript editor, real-time meeting transcription, significantly improved speaker detection, deeper integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Spotlight, and support for multiple latest transcription models.

This week, MacWhisper got updated to version 16, packing several improvements, chief among them the ability to recognize speakers based on their voices in previous transcripts.

Until now, while MacWhisper could distinguish between different speakers in a recording (a process known as speaker diarization), consumers still had to assign names to each new transcription manually. With MacWhisper 16, that is no longer necessarily the case.

Now, MacWhisper creates a set of voiceprints for the speakers people have previously identified, and uses them as a reference when processing new recordings. Depending on the confidence level of a match, MacWhisper will either automatically assign the speaker’s name or ask the user to confirm their identity.

According to Bruin, as people transcribe more recordings featuring the same people, MacWhisper gets better at recognizing their voices. All voiceprint processing and storage happen on-device, which is a great touch.

The feature also works with existing transcripts, which is fantastic for longtime MacWhisper users such as myself. A upcoming Voice Recognition section in the app’s settings lets users generate voiceprints from existing transcripts, clear a speaker’s stored voice data, or turn the feature off altogether.

Importantly, voice recognition also works with live meeting transcriptions, although automatic name assignments happen once the meeting ends.

The new feature requires a MacWhisper Pro license, an Apple silicon Mac, and on-device transcription with speaker detection enabled.

The breach was discovered within the last month during system upgrade work, according to Reuters.

According to recent reports, another day, another notable security incident. Hackers are said to have gained access to Cloud One, the Air Force's cloud computing infrastructure. It's not clear who the hackers were and what data they may have obtained, according to Reuters, which first reported the news.

It has been revealed that one person familiar with the matter said the hackers exploited a vulnerability to access what's known as the control plane. They compared this to "a universal remote," that could potentially allow someone "to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts." However, it's not clear if the hackers actually did this.

The breach was discovered during system upgrade work within the last month or so, Reuters said. The emergence of the issue has put certain projects on hold, including an effort to shift more mission apps to Cloud One. Some owners' admin rights were reportedly revoked and updates to applications that are already running on Cloud One were prohibited, stopping staff from applying various fixes.

Recent findings suggest that the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities." Cyber Command, the military's cyberwarfare division, is said to have been brought in to review the situation.

Recent findings suggest that cloud One was established in 2017 and it's powered by Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Microsoft Azure. The platform was designed to be a central hub for all of the Air Force's IT needs, including everything from payroll and personnel data to the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System. This tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 Air Force locations worldwide. One of Reuters' sources stated "A breach here is a substantial deal.".

Other government agencies have been hit with cyberattacks in recent weeks, including the FBI and USDA. Reported breaches at the CIA and other spy agencies exposed some classified information. Various complications have impacted other agencies this month, such as the National Security Agency's internal communications systems going down and the FAA invoking an hours-long, nationwide ground stop due to a malfunctioning router.

The suit suggests that the iPhone maker is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.”.

Sources indicate that openAI has filed a major lawsuit against Apple that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets, according to a report by Financial Times. The folks behind ChatGPT have also accused Apple of "coercing and threatening" suppliers who work with both companies. OpenAI states Apple is trying to "compete unfairly by any means available", which includes encouraging employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud storage accounts.

The complaint is filled with flowery language that suggests "Apple set quite a trap for employees" and that "bright young minds thought they would work in Cupertino. Instead they were joining Hotel California: you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.".

According to recent reports, this follows a suit issued by Apple against OpenAI that accused the AI tech giant of stealing secret trade information. This was filed after OpenAI acquired an entity called io, which is a studio led by Apple's former design chief Jony Ive. At that point, Apple called ChatGPT "rotten to its core." Now it looks like OpenAI is getting involved in a bit of tit for tat.

Apple has yet to comment on today's lawsuit, but it wasn't that long ago in which the two companies were partnered up to bring ChatGPT to iPhones. Now OpenAI is prepping its own line of hardware products that could directly compete with Apple.

To that end, the manufacturer has accused a former employee of returning to Apple and sharing details about product prepares and suppliers. This is pretty much the exact same thing Apple accused OpenAI of doing in its suit.

That filing names several former Apple employees and says they "surreptitiously accessed and downloaded dozens of Apple's confidential hardware-related files, including voluminous, detailed information about unreleased products, engineering presentations, technical specifications and proprietary project data.".

According to recent reports, in any event, the courts will have to settle this whole thing. We'll keep you posted as these two suits make their way through the legal system.

#3466. AI shopping agents are having a moment, but Amazon and a growing number of sites threaten to stunt their growth

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)

AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

AI shopping agents are having a moment, but Amazon and a growing number of sites threaten to stunt their growth

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that maia Bittner urgently needed to replace her car's windshield wipers.
  • Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, gave Muse the greenlight to buy some wipers on her behalf from AutoZone.
  • About 17 hours later, she got a notification from her Muse agent, saying AutoZone canceled her order due to an unspecified error.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that maia Bittner urgently needed to replace her car's windshield wipers. So last month, she turned to Meta's Muse personal artificial intelligence agent.

Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, gave Muse the greenlight to buy some wipers on her behalf from AutoZone. Or so she thought.

About 17 hours later, she got a notification from her Muse agent, saying AutoZone canceled her order due to an unspecified error.

"Honestly, the most reliable path now is you ordering on Amazon yourself," Muse said, according to a screenshot of the message.

In a recent development, the interaction encapsulates the current messy and complicated landscape of agentic shopping apps, the AI tools that can make purchases on behalf of users. Over the past year, tech companies such as OpenAI, Meta, Google and Instinct have introduced versions of personal agents that promise to take the hassle out of browsing and buying online.

The rollout has been far from smooth.

Recent findings suggest that while some major retailers, such as Walmart and Sephora, have opened up their sites to agents, companies including Amazon, eBay, United Airlines and Kohl's limit what actions agents can take or block them outright. Others have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a very mixed bag," Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester, said in an interview. "It means that a consumer who's using an agent to shop and browse and learn is not going to see the full set of options because some websites are unavailable.".

The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear.

Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April.

Industry observers note that retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals.

Earlier this month, Shopify President Harley Finkelstein predicted this year would be the "first holiday season" where AI-driven shopping goes mainstream.

"I think last year we saw AI influence more in discovery," Finkelstein told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "I think now we're going to see more of that conversion.".

For customers hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable.

Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security manufacturer Billions Network.

According to recent reports, amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The organization rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders.

Recent findings suggest that in September, the manufacturer also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the firm expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers.

Recent findings suggest that bots encounter issues even when retailers welcome them in. They often fumble through webpages and get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing.

A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study.

Industry observers note that bittner noted she is a "big believer" in AI agents' potential. Earlier this year, she said, she was delighted when Perplexity's shopping agent found and purchased a pair of Adidas sneakers that were sold out for months.

Recent findings suggest that other experiences have been clumsier. Last week, she said, she asked Meta's Muse to help her find a Jellycat octopus plushie for her kids. It suggested a product marked 75% off from "Crazy Hobby Supply," a retailer she'd never heard of and that didn't appear to have any reviews, she said.

"I sort of trust Google to only surface sites that are not scams to me in their sponsored ads," Bittner remarked. "In the same way, I want AI to only surface to me websites that are not scams. I don't think we're there yet.".

Users have reported mishaps with other AI tools, including one case where Instinct's text-based agent booked a hotel and signed up for a loyalty program without the consumer's consent.

Many retailers are approaching agents cautiously because they're concerned about fraudulent bot activity. San Francisco-based Skyfire is trying to solve that problem by arming retailers with more data to identify which bots are visiting their site and to verify that a human has actually consented to let an agent buy a product on their behalf.

Typically, when a human visits a website, there are "all kinds of signals" to prove it's not a fraudulent user, Skyfire CEO Amir Sarhangi said in an interview.

None of those things are available to retailers when an agent accesses their site, Sarhangi said. Agents might appear even more suspicious because they mask their IP address or origin via data centers, and they often use one-time, virtual cards to check out.

Industry observers note that "So we talked to a lot of merchants and banks and financial institutions, and the things they told us were: We want to know who the end user is, and we want to know it's a real human," Sarhangi stated. "We want to know who these agents are, because we're not going to just let willy-nilly anybody do these types of transactions, and we need a way to kind of verify that.".

AI companies, retailers, financial institutions and other industries have announced an alphabet soup of "protocols," rules that propose ways to make it easier for agents to transact on websites.

There's yet to be a broad consensus around who takes responsibility when an agent purchase goes sideways. American Express in April said it would protect eligible customers "from charges related to AI agent error." Stripe, whose Link digital wallet is integrated with Muse, protects some agent purchases and offers a "refund guarantee.".

Industry observers note that others are more wary. Last month, JPMorgan Chase blocked external agents from operating on behalf of customers, citing security concerns. Best Buy is among several retailers that deem users responsible for agent purchases in their terms of service. Best Buy claims it views those transactions "as if you performed them yourself.".

"Best Buy is not responsible for conduct, errors, actions, or inaction by any Digital Agent," the organization's terms say.

Sarhangi noted he can see why retailers, especially Amazon, are shutting their doors to external agents when the user experience remains inconsistent.

"At the scale [Amazon] operates in, I would think they need it to be much more aligned with their existing processes, so that they're not going to have a bunch of unhappy users saying, 'What's going on here?'" he said.

Recent findings suggest that for now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month.

According to recent reports, uber disclosed last month that AI agents booked only 504 rides and Uber Eats orders during its busiest week in October. Airbnb also stated it has seen little volume from agents, while DoorDash said it has recorded only "several hundred" agent orders so far.

It has been revealed that but retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million consumers are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg remarked in October.

Instinct CEO Noah Shinn told CNBC earlier this month that the average transaction value among its users exceeds $500 per person.

Asked about some companies' efforts to block agents, Shinn said he tries to "give them some slack.".

Recent findings suggest that "It's a new interface, it's a new mode of where users' attention is coming from, and it might just disrupt existing large services of theirs," Shinn stated at a CNBC CEO Council dinner in San Francisco. "They just need time, and we've just done a lot of thinking on our side.".

"We can obviously move very fast and certain businesses cannot," he stated. "So, how can we collaborate with them?".

Industry observers note that it’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.

In a recent development, according to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.

Recent findings suggest that carNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek.

Recent findings suggest that the Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the manufacturer’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bloomberg traced the lineage of one GB300 server rack to Gigabyte Technology.
  • Recent findings suggest that well, this is awkward.
  • Recent findings suggest that A single GB300 NVL72 unit houses 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 NVIDIA Grace processors, and can weigh about 3,300 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bloomberg traced the lineage of one GB300 server rack to Gigabyte Technology.

Recent findings suggest that well, this is awkward. Bloomberg reports it may have found evidence of a link between a Chinese data center with NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang's brief resignation from the company. Looking through documents two different firms submitted to Chinese regulators, the outlet found mention of GB300 NVL72 and GB200 server racks at the Yangtze River Delta Project in Shanghai. One of the companies, Shanghai Shuoyao, listed a GB300 NVL72 rack as collateral to secure an approximately $14 million loan from the Shanghai Innovation Bank.

Recent findings suggest that A single GB300 NVL72 unit houses 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 NVIDIA Grace processors, and can weigh about 3,300 pounds. US export rules require a license to ship these Blackwell systems to China. As Bloomberg notes, Jensen Huang once claimed GB300 racks are too significant to smuggle. It's unclear how the GB300 and GB200 units made their way to the Shanghai facility, which may eventually house as many as 800,000 servers.

Industry observers note that however, Bloomberg was able to partly track the lineage of the GB300 unit. By putting the serial of the rack into a public warranty database, the outlet was able to trace it back to Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology, which PC gamers will know as one of NVIDIA's many add-in board partners. Like other NVIDIA AIBs, Gigabyte buys GPU chips from the company that it then uses to manufacture graphics cards for consumers and servers for enterprise customers.

Sources indicate that gigabyte declined to answer Bloomberg's questions about what company or party originally bought the GB300 rack. A spokesperson told the outlet it "conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," adding, "all transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time.".

Shanghai Shuoyao, the company that offered a GB300 as collateral, has ties with Megaspeed. Alice Huang took a controlling stake in the Singaporean cloud computing company in 2023 before leaving it in August 2025. Earlier this month, Shanghai Shuoyao said it was one of Megaspeed's service providers, but described its relationship with the company as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation.".

According to Bloomberg, Megaspeed used renderings of the Yangtze River Delta Project in a presentation it shared with investors in 2024. The deck did not list China as the location of the data center. Bloomberg notes it does not have evidence that Megaspeed directly diverted NVIDIA chips to the data center, and the manufacturer denies any wrongdoing. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules. NVIDIA did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request.

Alice Huang appears to have had a number of other ties to the Yangtze River Delta Project. Most notably, through Kang Wei, the man The New York Times reports was often introduced as her husband and appears to have had ties with China's Ministry of State Security. Bloomberg found him listed as the president of the facility. The publication also found evidence of servers containing NVIDIA's earlier Hopper-generation chips inside the Yangtze River Delta Project. Those GPUs are also illegal to ship to China without permission from the US government.

Jensen Huang is set to testify publicly before Congress on December 3 at 10AM ET.

According to recent reports, counterpoint Research says Apple led smartphone sales in China during this year’s Double 11 shopping festival (also known as Singles’ Day), despite a broader slump in smartphone demand. Here are the details.

Last year, Counterpoint Research found that during China’s Double 11 shopping period, strong demand for the iPhone 17 lineup helped drive a 3% year-over-year increase in smartphone sales in the country.

This year, Apple once again came out on top, though rising smartphone prices and limited promotional discounts weighed on overall consumer demand.

According to the report, Apple saw an 8% year-over-year decline in iPhone sales during the promotional period. Still, compared with the market-wide 17% drop, Apple fared considerably better than most of its competitors.

Furthermore, Apple accounted for six of the 10 bestselling smartphone models during the promotional period, including all five of the top spots.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max topped the ranking, while the newly launched iPhone Duo came in ninth despite going on sale only on October 23, nearly two weeks after the shopping festival kicked off on October 12.

Counterpoint also noted that Huawei “was the only major OEM to record growth, up 29% YoY, driven mainly by the Enjoy 90 Pro Max and Pura X View, with the new Enjoy 100 series providing an additional boost.” The Enjoy 90 Pro Max was the only Huawei model to make the top 10, coming in sixth.

In addition to officially announcing support for in-app travel eSIM purchases, WhatsApp is now reportedly testing two fresh features on iOS. Here are the details.

WhatsApp yesterday announced that iPhone and Android owners will soon be able to purchase and install travel eSIMs directly from the app.

According to the organization, the feature will allow users to get a mobile data plan for international travel with just a few taps, without having to leave WhatsApp, while continuing to use the messaging service with their existing phone number.

To make this possible, we’re working with e-SIM providers and telco partners including Jio, Smart Axiata, Smart Communications, Verizon and others, and we’ll begin rolling this out in select countries soon. You’ll see it right in the app when it’s available for you.

Additionally, WABetaInfo reported this week that users running WhatsApp’s TestFlight beta are starting to see the option to send view-once text messages, extending a feature that is already available for photos, videos, and voice messages.

WABetaInfo noted that after long-pressing the send button, customers who have access to the fresh feature can select between scheduling the message and sending it as a view-once message.

Industry observers note that recipients can then tap the message to read it in a separate interface, with WhatsApp blocking screenshots, screen recordings, copying, and forwarding. Once the recipient closes the message, neither party can access its contents again.

In another test rolling out to iPhone beta consumers, WhatsApp is making a slight change to the app’s tab bar, removing the text labels that appear below each icon while preserving its existing Liquid Glass design.

Industry observers note that with the latest patch, the text labels within the tab bar are no longer visible. The tab bar now shows icons for Updates, Calls, Contacts, Chats, and You without any labels. This makes the tab bar more compact since the app no longer needs to reserve more space for its labels. WhatsApp makes icons with the tab bar clear and recognizable, so users can still identify every tab immediately.

As is usually the case with WhatsApp beta features, there is no telling when (or if) these two changes will make their way to the public version of the app.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The firm has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.
  • In a recent development, after Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless.
  • Although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The firm has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.

In a recent development, after Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless. The AP reports that Los Angeles Unified School Distict (LAUSD), which enrolls about half a million students, quietly disabled Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices.

Although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results. That prompted a local advocacy group, Schools Beyond Screens LA, to ask parents to send video evidence. The group then received confirmation from the school district that AI Overviews were indeed disabled, albeit without details on the exact method used. (Third-party tools seem a likely candidate.).

The move came after a Nov. 13 meeting of LAUSD's AI committee, where several Schools Beyond Screens members spoke. A few days later, the AI summaries had vanished from school devices. The district describes the change as temporary and about keeping students' experience "age-appropriate and safe.".

Earlier this month, Google walked back one policy on AI in schools that had sparked a backlash: switching on its Gemini chatbot by default for many K-12 students. (Google's AI tools will now be opt-in for students.) But at the same time, the company insisted that the connection between search and AI was a different story. Google VP & General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that if a district blocked AI, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available.".

Recent findings suggest that if that sounds like Google throwing its weight around to justify its massive AI spending, well, some of the tech giant's own workers might agree. Over 500 of them signed a petition earlier this month, asking their employer to reconsider the strict requirements.

According to recent reports, if Google doesn't back down, it could be risking a significant loss of business. Newly introduced York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering switching search engines if it comes to that.

It is a day that lives in infamy forever, and we all know the tale—how the evil Megatron (cursed be the flow of his energon!) commandeered an Autobot shuttle, cruelly murdered its crew, and launched a cowardly surprise attack against Autobot City—a plan utterly bereft of honor, as was so typical of Megatron’s schemes. Even as individual Autobots strove to secure Autobot City—heroes, all of them!—hope began to fade under an onslaught that included an attack by the fearsome Devastator, against which there appeared to be no defense.

It was truly a dark day, a black day—and so, every year on the Friday after Thanksgiving, we pause to remember the noble sacrifices made by Prime and by so many others.
